content: Healthcare providers who deliver care to children and adolescents should be equipped to recognize and manage tuberculosis (TB). The concept of task-shifting, as highlighted by the Guideline Development Group (GDG), is a critical factor in implementing effective TB care. Family-centered and integrated care is essential in child health, but the definition of family-centered care remains unclear. This approach is closely related to patient-centered care, which systematically assesses and addresses the needs and expectations of patients. The End TB Strategy emphasizes providing high-quality TB diagnosis and treatment to all patients—men, women, and children—without imposing catastrophic costs. Depending on individual patient needs, educational, emotional, and economic support should be provided to ensure completion of the diagnostic process and prescribed treatment. Family-centered care also involves household-level interventions to identify members who may require TB evaluation, preventive therapy (TPT), or treatment support. Since the concept of family-centered, integrated care may vary by setting, it is important to clarify its definition and tailor implementation strategies to the specific social, cultural, and societal values of the country or region. National TB programs should define and develop a package of TB services in coordination with other relevant programs, such as child and adolescent TB technical working groups. This package should address capacity needs and be informed by family and community perceptions of the ideal care model. Community-based models can be included in this package, such as active contact investigation, identifying children with TB symptoms or exposure during routine growth-monitoring services, or integrating TB care into the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework. Integration can begin within families by educating them to recognize TB symptoms, understand the importance of contact history, seek timely healthcare, and reduce TB-related stigma. High-yield entry points within the health system, such as malnutrition clinics, antenatal care (ANC), immunization programs, and pediatric clinics, can serve as starting points for integrating child and adolescent TB services. Ideally, TB care should be integrated into general health services rather than relying solely on coordination between separate programs. Defining optimal patient flow between services and establishing strong links between child health entry points and TB clinics is essential, particularly in facilities where services are physically separated. This integration improves service quality, ensures accurate record-keeping, and facilitates follow-up during diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Pilot programs can be initiated to test and refine these approaches before scaling up. Factors such as baseline health infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, financing, human resource needs, and community perceptions should be considered. Monitoring and evaluation are critical to assess the implementation of decentralized, family-centered, and integrated services. Enhanced data collection on child and adolescent TB, including disaggregated data by sex, is necessary to evaluate gender equity and service quality. Programs should also monitor the number of children diagnosed at different health system levels, the proportion with bacteriological confirmation, and those completing TPT. Research priorities include evaluating interventions to improve treatment adherence, patient support, and supervision, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Cost-effectiveness analyses of incentives and decentralized care models are needed, as well as studies on the psychological support required for TB patients. Programs should systematically collect and publish data on decentralized care to inform best practices. Family-centered, integrated services for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure should be described in detail, including associated costs and cost-effectiveness. Implementation research should assess the feasibility and acceptability of these approaches from the perspectives of patients, caregivers, and providers. Outcomes of interest include TPT initiation, additional diagnoses, treatment completion, clinical outcomes, and qualitative research on stigma, mental health, and equity. Randomized and non-randomized studies, as well as community needs assessments, are essential to improve TB care and prevention for children and adolescents.
